Sub-Area Level Estimation with Two-Fold Models

Source: vignettes/twofold-subarea.Rmd
twofold-subarea.Rmd

Overview

Surveys are often designed for large areas (provinces, regions) but the estimates are needed for the sub-areas inside them (districts, municipalities). The sub-areas of one area share the area’s characteristics, so their estimates should borrow strength not only from the regression on auxiliary variables, but also from the other sub-areas of the same area.

The two-fold sub-area level model of Torabi and Rao (2014) does this with two nested random effects. fastsae fits it in two ways:

Function Approach Uncertainty Area aggregates
eblup_twofold() EBLUP, REML or ML Analytical (Prasad-Rao type) or parametric bootstrap MSE df_area, weighted by weight
hb_twofold() Hierarchical Bayes with INLA Posterior SD and credible intervals df_area, weighted by weight

hb_twofold() also fits binomial and Poisson responses and a spatial (BYM2, Besag) area effect.

Model

For sub-area jj (j=1,…,Nij = 1, \dots, N_i) of area ii (i=1,…,mi = 1, \dots, m), the direct estimator yijy_{ij} with known sampling variance ψij\psi_{ij} follows

yij=θij+eij,θij=xij⊤β+vi+uij,y_{ij} = \theta_{ij} + e_{ij}, \qquad \theta_{ij} = x_{ij}^\top \beta + v_i + u_{ij},

with vi∼N(0,σv2)v_i \sim N(0, \sigma_v^2) the area effect, uij∼N(0,σu2)u_{ij} \sim N(0, \sigma_u^2) the sub-area effect and eij∼N(0,ψij)e_{ij} \sim N(0, \psi_{ij}) the sampling error, all independent.

Compared with the Fay-Herriot model, which treats every sub-area as unrelated, the area effect viv_i is estimated from all the sampled sub-areas of area ii. This matters most for sub-areas that are not sampled: they get xij⊤β̂+v̂ix_{ij}^\top \hat\beta + \hat v_i instead of the synthetic xij⊤β̂x_{ij}^\top \hat\beta alone. Only a sub-area of an area without any sample is predicted synthetically.

The output follows the notation above: random_effect_var holds sigma2_v (area) and sigma2_u (sub-area), and df_eblup (or df_hb) holds random_effect_area and random_effect_subarea.

Example with simulated data

We simulate 30 areas with 3 to 6 sub-areas each, so that the true sub-area means θij\theta_{ij} are known. Fifteen sub-areas have no sample (their direct estimate is NA), and all the sub-areas of area A30 are unsampled.

library(fastsae)

set.seed(2024)
m <- 30
dat <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(m), function(i) {
  ni <- sample(3:6, 1)
  data.frame(
    area = sprintf("A%02d", i),
    subarea = sprintf("A%02d-%d", i, seq_len(ni)),
    x1 = rnorm(ni, mean = 2),
    pop = sample(200:2000, ni)
  )
}))
v <- rnorm(m, sd = 1)
names(v) <- unique(dat$area)
dat$theta <- 10 + 2 * dat$x1 + v[dat$area] + rnorm(nrow(dat), sd = sqrt(0.5))
dat$vardir <- runif(nrow(dat), 0.5, 2)
dat$y <- dat$theta + rnorm(nrow(dat), sd = sqrt(dat$vardir))

# Unsampled sub-areas: 15 at random, plus every sub-area of A30
unsampled <- union(sample(which(dat$area != "A30"), 15), which(dat$area == "A30"))
dat$y[unsampled] <- NA

c(subareas = nrow(dat), sampled = sum(!is.na(dat$y)))
#> subareas  sampled 
#>      131      111
head(dat)
#>   area subarea        x1  pop    theta   vardir        y
#> 1  A01   A01-1 1.5347257 1857 13.78128 1.663801 12.20118
#> 2  A01   A01-2 2.5191534 1961 15.03099 1.105026 14.48113
#> 3  A01   A01-3 2.5284898 1222 14.79953 1.301555 15.01471
#> 4  A01   A01-4 1.4848072 1252 11.84648 1.406429 11.36094
#> 5  A02   A02-1 1.8729653 1255 13.61192 1.986447 12.02304
#> 6  A02   A02-2 0.7751246  924 12.23727 1.268523       NA

Each row is one sub-area. Unsampled sub-areas stay in the data with y = NA and their covariates, so that they are predicted.

Fitting the EBLUP 

fit_tf <- eblup_twofold(
  y ~ x1,
  vardir = "vardir",
  domain = "area",
  subarea = "subarea",
  data = dat,
  weight = "pop",
  print_result = FALSE
)

fit_tf$random_effect_var
#>  sigma2_v  sigma2_u 
#> 1.1067031 0.1486881
fit_tf$estcoef
#>                 beta std.error stderr_beta   zvalue        pvalue
#> (Intercept) 9.605159 0.3223129   0.3223129 29.80073 3.822665e-195
#> x1          2.104314 0.1144109   0.1144109 18.39260  1.505751e-75
head(fit_tf$df_eblup)
#>   domain subarea        y    eblup   vardir random_effect_area
#> 1    A01   A01-1 12.20118 12.39678 1.663801         -0.4204473
#> 2    A01   A01-2 14.48113 14.48525 1.105026         -0.4204473
#> 3    A01   A01-3 15.01471 14.55766 1.301555         -0.4204473
#> 4    A01   A01-4 11.36094 12.21855 1.406429         -0.4204473
#> 5    A02   A02-1 12.02304 12.66335 1.986447         -0.8351927
#> 6    A02   A02-2       NA 10.40107 1.268523         -0.8351927
#>   random_effect_subarea       mse      rse
#> 1         -0.0174796591 0.4205889 5.231427
#> 2         -0.0005543296 0.3941804 4.334326
#> 3          0.0522123369 0.4063272 4.378712
#> 4         -0.0906664052 0.4122688 5.254976
#> 5         -0.0479275040 0.4428309 5.254973
#> 6          0.0000000000 0.4782345 6.648787

The default mse_type = "analytical" gives the Prasad-Rao type MSE of the REML fit (for ML it adds the bias correction). Sub-area A01-3 is not sampled: it still gets the area effect of A01, while its sub-area effect is 0.

weight (here the population of each sub-area) aggregates the sub-area EBLUPs to area means, θ̃i=∑jwijθ̃ij/∑jwij\tilde\theta_i = \sum_j w_{ij}\tilde\theta_{ij} / \sum_j w_{ij}, in df_area. Their MSE accounts for the errors the sub-areas of an area share (the estimated area effect and β̂\hat\beta), so it is larger than ∑jwij2mseij\sum_j w_{ij}^2\,\mathrm{mse}_{ij} would suggest.

head(fit_tf$df_area)
#>   domain eblup_area  mse_area rse_area n_subareas n_sampled
#> 1    A01   13.43189 0.2748473 3.903090          4         4
#> 2    A02   11.19056 0.3146821 5.012844          5         4
#> 3    A03   14.07817 0.2208185 3.337885          3         3
#> 4    A04   16.64890 0.3174408 3.384120          6         4
#> 5    A05   13.25981 0.4443843 5.027383          4         3
#> 6    A06   12.79993 0.2838182 4.162101          3         3

How much does the area effect help?

Because the data are simulated, we can compare each estimator with the true θij\theta_{ij}. The Fay-Herriot model, fitted with eblup_fh() on the same rows, ignores the areas.

fit_fh <- eblup_fh(y ~ x1, vardir = "vardir", data = dat, print_result = FALSE)

sampled <- !is.na(dat$y)
in_sampled_area <- !sampled & dat$area != "A30"
emp_mse <- function(est, rows) mean((est[rows] - dat$theta[rows])^2)

data.frame(
  rows = c("sampled sub-areas", "unsampled sub-areas of sampled areas"),
  direct = c(emp_mse(dat$y, sampled), NA),
  fay_herriot = c(
    emp_mse(fit_fh$df_eblup$eblup, sampled),
    emp_mse(fit_fh$df_eblup$eblup, in_sampled_area)
  ),
  two_fold = c(
    emp_mse(fit_tf$df_eblup$eblup, sampled),
    emp_mse(fit_tf$df_eblup$eblup, in_sampled_area)
  )
)
#>                                   rows   direct fay_herriot  two_fold
#> 1                    sampled sub-areas 1.211463   0.5087563 0.5291281
#> 2 unsampled sub-areas of sampled areas       NA   1.5247133 0.7748664

Both models improve on the direct estimates of the sampled sub-areas, and in this data set they are about equally accurate there: a sampled sub-area has its own direct estimate, so the area effect adds little. The difference is in the unsampled sub-areas of sampled areas. The Fay-Herriot model can only give them the synthetic estimate, while the two-fold model adds the estimated area effect and roughly halves the error. This is one simulated data set, not a simulation study: the gain depends on how large σv2\sigma_v^2 is relative to σu2\sigma_u^2.

Bootstrap MSE

The parametric bootstrap refits the model on B data sets generated from the fitted model and predicts with the same estimator as the point estimate. seed makes it reproducible without changing the random number stream of the session.

fit_boot <- eblup_twofold(
  y ~ x1,
  vardir = "vardir",
  domain = "area",
  subarea = "subarea",
  data = dat,
  mse_type = "bootstrap",
  B = 100,
  seed = 1,
  print_result = FALSE
)

summary(fit_boot$df_eblup$mse / fit_tf$df_eblup$mse)
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>  0.6322  0.8257  0.9056  0.9205  0.9971  1.4684

The two MSE estimators agree on average; with B = 100 single bootstrap values are still noisy. Use mse_type = "none" when only the point estimates are needed.

Diagnostics and plots

The usual tools of the package work on the result:

autoplot(fit_tf, type = "comparison")

diagnose(fit_tf)
#> ── fastsae Small Area Estimation Diagnostic Report ─────────────────────────────

Hierarchical Bayes with hb_twofold()

hb_twofold() fits the same model with INLA. It needs the INLA package, which is not on CRAN; see https://www.r-inla.org/download/. The chunks below are only run when INLA is installed.

The argument weight (here the population of each sub-area) aggregates the sub-area posteriors to area estimates, θ̂i=∑jwijθij/∑jwij\hat\theta_i = \sum_j w_{ij} \theta_{ij} / \sum_j w_{ij}, with their posterior uncertainty in df_area.

fit_hb <- hb_twofold(
  y ~ x1,
  vardir = "vardir",
  domain = "area",
  subarea = "subarea",
  weight = "pop",
  data = dat,
  print_result = FALSE
)

fit_hb$random_effect_var
#>  sigma2_v  sigma2_u 
#> 1.2370025 0.1859788
head(fit_hb$df_hb)
#>   domain subarea        y       hb linear_pred   vardir        sd       mse

With the default vague priors the posterior means are very close to the EBLUP:

cor(fit_tf$df_eblup$eblup, fit_hb$df_hb$hb)
#> [1] 0.999991
compare_sae(fit_tf, fit_hb, names = c("EBLUP two-fold", "HB two-fold"))
#> 
#> ── Small Area Estimation Model Concordance & Comparison ────────────────────────
#> Model 1: EBLUP two-fold
#> Model 2: HB two-fold
#> Matched Domains: 131
#> ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> 
#> Key Concordance & Efficiency Metrics:
#>                                                    Metric     Value
#>                                           Matched Domains       131
#>                                   Pearson Correlation (r)    1.0000
#>                                Spearman Correlation (rho)    0.9999
#>                            Mean Absolute Difference (MAE)    0.0077
#>                       Root Mean Squared Difference (RMSD)    0.0104
#>             Mean MSE Ratio (EBLUP two-fold / HB two-fold)    1.0438
#>           Median MSE Ratio (EBLUP two-fold / HB two-fold)    1.0526
#>       Domains where HB two-fold reports lower uncertainty 103 / 131
#>  % of domains where HB two-fold reports lower uncertainty     78.6%
#>                               Mean RSE % (EBLUP two-fold)     4.97%
#>                                  Mean RSE % (HB two-fold)     4.89%
#>                                 Average RSE Reduction (%)     0.08%
#> ℹ One model is Hierarchical Bayes: its posterior variance and the frequentist MSE of the other are not the same quantity, so a smaller value does not show a more accurate estimator.

compare_sae() reports smaller posterior variances than EBLUP MSEs. The two are not the same quantity, and here the posterior mean of σu2\sigma_u^2 is also smaller than the REML estimate (both are below the true value 0.5, which is hard to separate from sampling variances of 0.5 to 2). A smaller reported uncertainty is therefore not evidence of a more accurate estimator. With simulated data, the error against the truth settles it; here the two are practically equal:

c(
  eblup_two_fold = emp_mse(fit_tf$df_eblup$eblup, sampled | in_sampled_area),
  hb_two_fold = emp_mse(fit_hb$df_hb$hb, sampled | in_sampled_area)
)
#> eblup_two_fold    hb_two_fold 
#>      0.5583827      0.5570989

For counts or proportions, use family = "poisson" with exposure or family = "binomial" with trials; with spatial = "bym2" and a neighbourhood graph W between areas (for example from create_weights()), the area effects are spatially correlated.

MCMC with engine = jax_engine()

The same model can be sampled by MCMC (NumPyro’s No-U-Turn sampler on JAX) instead of INLA. It needs Python with jax and numpyro (see ?setup_numpyro_env), so this chunk is not run here. The result has the same structure, plus the posterior draws in draws and the largest split R-hat in rhat_max; the area aggregates in df_area come from the MCMC draws.

fit_jax <- hb_twofold(
  y ~ x1,
  vardir = "vardir",
  domain = "area",
  subarea = "subarea",
  weight = "pop",
  data = dat,
  engine = jax_engine(warmup = 1000, samples = 1000, chains = 4),
  print_result = FALSE
)
fit_jax$rhat_max
head(fit_jax$df_area)

Both engines use the same priors by default (jax_engine(priors = "inla")), so their estimates differ only by INLA’s approximation and the Monte Carlo error.

Practical notes

  • Give one row per sub-area. The domain column identifies the area and is required.
  • vardir must be finite and positive for every sampled sub-area; unsampled sub-areas can have NA. Covariates must be complete for all rows, sampled or not.
  • At least two areas need sampled sub-areas, otherwise σv2\sigma_v^2 cannot be estimated.
  • eblup_twofold() has self_benchmark = TRUE for estimates that add up to a known total (see ?eblup_twofold).

References

  • Torabi, M., & Rao, J. N. K. (2014). On small area estimation under a sub-area level model. Journal of Multivariate Analysis, 127, 36–55.
  • Rao, J. N. K., & Molina, I. (2015). Small Area Estimation (2nd ed.). John Wiley & Sons.
  • Rue, H., Martino, S., & Chopin, N. (2009). Approximate Bayesian inference for latent Gaussian models by using integrated nested Laplace approximations. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B, 71(2), 319–392.
